meta.title: Technology and AI politics knowledge network, c. 1980-2026
meta.description: Key works and debates on the politics of technology and artificial intelligence: platform power and governance, algorithmic power and accountability, AI ethics and alignment, algorithmic fairness, surveillance and privacy, digital authoritarianism, misinformation and bots, social media and the public sphere, digital activism, digital campaigns, digital divides, automation and the political economy of AI, digital government, regulating technology, cyber conflict and military AI, tech geopolitics, and computational social science. Seeds come from this repo's papers.json; works shared with the other maps are imported from them; others are top-cited 2006-2026 articles selected via Crossref (thirteen technology, communication and AI-ethics journals plus political science and economics journals) and anchoring books and classics. Direction: source (later or dependent work) -> target (earlier or anchoring work).

edge_types.builds_on: source extends or relies on target's argument or evidence
edge_types.challenges: source contests target's claim, mechanism or evidence
edge_types.qualifies: source adds a scope condition or moderating factor to target
edge_types.extends_to_new_case: source applies target's logic to a new population, period or domain
edge_types.synthesizes: source integrates target with other work
edge_types.mechanism_tested_by: source tests a mechanism implied by target

meta.verification: Repo works come from the user's Zotero library. Works imported from the other maps keep their verification. Crossref-selected works take title, authors, year, venue and DOI from Crossref records. Anchors are checked in Crossref separately; see each node's `verified` field. One-line claims for non-repo works are my summaries.

edges.why: Networked production and code as regulation.
Content moderation is what platforms do.
Documents data-driven microtargeting of divisive Facebook ads by anonymous groups, extending work on technology-intensive campaigning.
Ethnographic comparison of how algorithms are used in newsrooms and courts, studying algorithms as practice.
Extends critical race analysis of technology to the racialized imagery of AI.
Develops concern about humans held liable without real control into a typology of four AI responsibility gaps.
Proves that calibration and balance conditions for fair risk scores cannot all hold at once.
Racial bias in a health algorithm.
Treats propaganda as speech that undermines the reasonable deliberation democratic legitimacy depends on.
Tests why people believe the partisan fake news seen in 2016, pointing to lack of reasoning rather than motivated reasoning.
Warns that online communication fragments the public into isolated issue publics.
Meta-analysis of whether internet use boosts civic engagement, the question at the center of Norris's digital-divide debate.
Obama campaigns adapted to a hybrid, personalized communication environment.
Online participation as a distinct mode.
Links automation-driven occupational decline to status loss and support for the populist right.
Review of workplace technology and politics.
AI challenges in the public sector.
US and EU AI regulation compared.
Defines social media services as a basis for governing them, extending debate over what platforms are.
Cyber war will not take place.
Uses Stuxnet to show the practical limits of cyber weapons.
AI and the balance of power.
Prediction versus judgment in military AI.
Both treat control over technology and economic networks as a source of coercive leverage in great-power rivalry.
Treats the demographic biases critics flag in language models as a usable reflection of subgroup opinion.
